summary: A US envoy says the Iran war could last a year, Israel seals Hebron before its vote, Brazil chooses a president, and a study counts Europe's summer heat deaths.

topics.heading: US envoy says the Iran war could last another year as oil hits a wartime high
topics.summary: Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, told the Financial Times the war could go on for a year and the US can keep blockading Iran's ports. Brent crude briefly passed $117 after Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed to have disabled seven tankers.

lead.title: Iran war could last another year, Trump ambassador says

alsoReported.title: Iran War Updates: Trump's U.N. ambassador says war could last another year as oil prices continue rising

article: In an interview with the Financial Times published Friday, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations, said the war with Iran could last another year[^1][^2]. He said the US Navy can keep up its blockade of Iranian ports "for the foreseeable future" and that economic pressure is being tightened, while adding he hoped Iran would "come to the table" before then[^1][^2].

Background: the US and Israel began the war with strikes on February 28, and the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route for much of the world's oil, has been disrupted since[^1]. This week Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck four ships and that three more hit mines; those claims had not been confirmed[^2]. Iranian state TV said all "non-compliant" ships had been stopped from crossing[^2]. Trump called the claims lies meant to push up oil prices before the US midterms[^2].

Markets reacted anyway. Brent crude, the global benchmark, briefly passed $117 a barrel on Friday, up from under $97 at the start of October[^2]. US regular gasoline averaged about $4.29 a gallon and diesel about $6.31, according to AAA figures cited by Salon[^1]. Saudi Aramco says it has raised its pipeline capacity to the Red Sea, which bypasses the strait, to 7 million barrels a day[^2].

There are mixed signals on what comes next. Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey, said a strike "this weekend" is possible, though Trump has said there would be none before the November 3 midterms[^2]. The State Department is reducing staff at embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE, and Iran's foreign minister says President Masoud Pezeshkian will visit Moscow next week[^2].

My read: a long stalemate, with a blockade on one side and ship attacks on the other, now looks like Washington's working assumption. That matters far beyond the Gulf, because fuel prices feed into food, transport and interest rates almost everywhere, including Canada.
topics.differences: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they disabled seven ships; this was unconfirmed, and Trump calls it a lie aimed at raising oil prices[^2]. Waltz says the war could last a year, while Trump has said there will be no new strikes before the midterms and Ambassador Barrack says one is possible this weekend[^2].

topics.heading: Israel seals Hebron and readies a West Bank lockdown after two soldiers are killed
topics.summary: After two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers near Hebron, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the city sealed and a large operation prepared, four days before Israel's general election.

lead.title: Israel preparing full lockdown of occupied West Bank after Hebron gunfight

alsoReported.title: Israel's Netanyahu vows major military operation, cordons off West Bank city after deadly attack on troops
Benjamin Netanyahu seizes on Hebron attack to mount major West Bank offensive

article: On Friday, two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on Israeli troops at a junction near Hebron, a city of more than 200,000 people in the occupied West Bank[^5]. The Israeli military says two soldiers were killed and three lightly injured, and that both gunmen were killed[^5]. It says weapons and ammunition found in their car show they were planning a larger attack on civilians[^5]. Hamas and other armed groups praised the attack[^4].

Netanyahu ordered Hebron sealed and told security forces to prepare a full lockdown of the West Bank[^4]. He said troops would evacuate the gunmen's neighbourhood and search house to house for weapons, and described a broader operation in the West Bank[^5][^3]. He also called the attack an attempt to influence Israel's election[^5]. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for Israel to take full control of the West Bank and dismantle the Palestinian Authority[^4].

Background: the West Bank is the larger of the two Palestinian territories, and Israel has built settlements there that international law regards as illegal; Netanyahu has vowed to expand them faster[^3]. Violence there has risen during the Gaza war. On Thursday, Israeli forces arrested 36 Palestinians in raids, and a Palestinian commission recorded 17 attacks by settlers and soldiers on farmers during the olive harvest[^4].

Israelis vote on Tuesday, October 27, in the first general election since the October 7, 2023 attack[^3]. Netanyahu cancelled campaign events and went to the scene[^4]. Australia's ABC reports that his responsibility for the security failures before October 7 is a central campaign issue, and that some worry rising violence could help him look stronger on security[^3].

What to watch: whether the lockdown and the larger operation go ahead, and whether they spread to other cities. A big operation in the days before the vote would shape both the campaign and daily life for Palestinians across the territory.
topics.differences: The Israeli military says the gunmen planned a mass attack on civilians[^5]; Hamas and other Palestinian factions praised the attack as a response to Israeli raids and settler violence[^4]. Netanyahu says the attack aimed to influence the election, while ABC reports concern that the violence could strengthen his own campaign[^5][^3].

topics.heading: Russia and Ukraine agree to a local ceasefire in Oleshky, with wider talks next month
topics.summary: Both sides confirmed a truce in the occupied town of Oleshky so civilians can leave and aid can arrive, brokered with Melania Trump's help. Putin said wider US-mediated talks can resume next month.

lead.title: Ukraine confirms Oleshky ceasefire mediated by Melania Trump between Russia, Ukraine

alsoReported.title: Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, White House says
Putin Says Renewed Peace Talks Must Focus on Security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe Overall

article: The White House said on Friday that First Lady Melania Trump had mediated a local ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region[^7]. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed it, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised her "significant contribution"[^6]. The aim is to let civilians leave safely and let humanitarian aid in[^6].

Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from Ukrainian-held Kherson. It had about 24,000 people before the invasion; the White House estimates 1,700 to 2,000 remain, including about 50 children[^7]. Ukraine says Russian forces have blocked aid, and people trying to leave face mined roads and drone attacks[^6][^7]. Euronews notes it could not verify conditions there, because independent journalists cannot enter[^7].

Under the plan, fighting stops in and around the town, aid is delivered, and residents may leave for Russia or Ukraine, as they choose[^6]. Ukraine's General Staff says the truce starts early on October 27[^6]. Lubinets warned it will be "extremely difficult to implement," and an aid volunteer told the Kyiv Independent he feared provocations[^6]. A wider energy truce announced on October 13 did not hold in practice[^6].

The bigger picture: Putin said on Thursday that Russia is ready to resume US-mediated talks next month, and that they should cover security guarantees for both countries and Europe's security as a whole[^8]. He wants a lasting settlement, not a short ceasefire, and repeated his claim that Ukraine's eastern Donbas region is "historical Russia"[^8]. Ukraine rejects giving up land it holds, which remains the main gap[^8].

My read: a one-town truce is small, but if it works, it is the kind of practical step that can build some trust before larger talks. If it fails, it will add to doubts about every promise made so far.
topics.differences: Ukraine's General Staff says the truce begins on October 27[^6], while Euronews, citing the White House, gives October 29[^7]. Russia says it wants Ukraine to give up all of Donbas; Ukraine refuses to hand over territory it controls[^8].

topics.heading: Brazil holds a tight presidential runoff on Sunday: Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
topics.summary: President Lula, 80, faces senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former president, in Sunday's runoff. The latest Datafolha poll shows a 50-50 tie after the two met in a final debate on Friday.

lead.title: Lula, Bolsonaro lock horns in final debate before Brazil vote

alsoReported.title: Why Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in Brazil's election

article: Brazil votes on Sunday, October 25, in a presidential runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, of the left-wing Workers' Party, and senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, of the right-wing Liberal Party[^10]. In the first round on October 4, Flávio Bolsonaro unexpectedly came first with about 47% to Lula's 45%; most polls had put Lula ahead[^10][^11].

Flávio is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a sentence of more than 27 years after the Supreme Court convicted him of plotting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula; he denies the charges[^9][^10]. Flávio has promised to pardon him[^10]. A Datafolha poll published Thursday showed a 50-50 tie, after Flávio had led by four points two weeks earlier[^9].

The candidates offer different paths. Flávio promises to cut spending and ministries, add 500,000 prison places, and repair ties with Washington; Lula promises tax exemptions for lower earners paid for by taxing the very rich, zero deforestation by 2030, and stresses Brazil's independence in trade[^9][^10]. Voters feel squeezed by food prices and debt, even though unemployment is at a record low[^11].

The campaign has been bitter. Both sides accuse each other of spreading false information, and both have gone to court over social media abuses[^9]. Lula's campaign accuses Meta of favouring his opponent; Meta denies it but admitted some Lula ads were wrongly switched off[^9].

Why it matters: the winner, who takes office on January 5, will shape policy on the Amazon rainforest, trade with the US and China, and Brazil's place in the BRICS group[^10]. Watch also how the loser and his supporters accept the result, given what happened after 2022.
topics.differences: Lula's campaign says Meta is interfering in Flávio Bolsonaro's favour; Meta denies it[^9]. Jair Bolsonaro's conviction is described by the courts as an attempted coup; he denies the charges[^10].

topics.heading: Study estimates Europe's summer heat killed about 50,000 people in its cities
topics.summary: Scientists estimate about 50,400 heat-related deaths in 854 European cities this summer, the most in at least 26 years, and attribute about two-thirds of them to human-caused warming.

lead.title: Europe's killer heat this summer claims 50,000 lives. Climate change blamed for two-thirds of deaths

article: Researchers at Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine estimate that heat killed about 50,391 people in 854 European cities between June and August this year[^12][^13]. They say about 32,600 of those deaths, roughly two-thirds, would not have happened without the extra heat from human-caused warming, mainly from burning fossil fuels[^12]. The work appears in two peer-reviewed papers in the journal Nature Health[^13].

That is the highest figure in the study's 26-year record. The next worst summer, 2022, had about 29,500 deaths[^12]. About a third of this year's deaths came during a heat wave from June 17 to July 1, when temperatures ran more than 5°C above normal[^12][^13]. Italy, France, Spain and Germany had the highest tolls[^12]. More than half of the dead were 85 or older, but about 6,000 were under 65[^12][^13].

How do scientists count this? Heat is rarely written on death certificates, so the team used statistical models that compare how many people died on hot days with how many usually would. To estimate the climate share, they compared real temperatures with simulations of a world without warming[^12]. Outside experts called the methods state of the art, and the authors say results mostly matched official estimates where those exist[^12].

The authors say the real toll is likely higher, because the study covers only cities holding about 40% of Europe's people and leaves out a deadly May heat wave[^12]. Researchers argue that cities are poorly adapted to rising heat and need more shade, cooling and early warnings[^13].

Why it matters for Canada: Canadian cities face hotter summers too, and the same lesson applies. Heat is a quiet killer, mostly of older and isolated people, and much of the risk can be reduced with planning.

topics.heading: Microsoft says its AI diagnosed hard medical cases better than general doctors in a test
topics.summary: In a study published in Science, Microsoft's MAI-DxO system correctly diagnosed 83% of complex simulated cases, against 36% for general doctors. The test used simulations, not real patients, and did not include specialists.

lead.title: Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases 'medical superintelligence'

alsoReported.title: Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose 'sequentially' like a doctor

article: Microsoft researchers published a study in the journal Science on Thursday about MAI-DxO, an AI system that diagnoses step by step, the way a doctor does: it asks questions, decides which tests to order, and then gives a diagnosis[^14][^15]. Inside, several AI agents act like a panel of doctors who debate the case[^14].

The test used more than 300 unusual, complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, turned into simulations[^15]. MAI-DxO got the diagnosis right 83% of the time; general doctors working alone with reference books and the internet got 36%[^14][^15]. The AI's workups also cost less[^15].

There are important limits. These were simulated patients, not real ones[^14]. The doctors were generalists, while cases this hard are usually handled by specialists or teams, who were not tested[^14]. Most of the gain came from the underlying AI models, such as OpenAI's GPT-5, rather than Microsoft's system on top[^14]. On emergency-room cases, the system added little[^14]. And the research was done by the company that makes the tool[^15].

Next, Microsoft will test it with consenting patients at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, comparing its advice with doctors' in parallel, and will look at triage in emergency waiting rooms[^14][^15]. Microsoft's Dominic King says the biggest problem in health care is that demand for medical expertise is outgrowing supply[^14].

My read: results like this are a real signal that AI could help with diagnosis, especially where doctors are scarce. But the step from a lab test to safe use in hospitals is long, and independent trials on real patients will matter more than any company benchmark.

question.text: Today's numbers include modelled heat deaths, unverified ship attacks, conditions in a town closed to reporters, an AI tested on simulated patients, and polls that missed Brazil's first round. Which one would you trust most, which least, and what would change your mind?
